content: Coffea, a genus of flowering plants in the Rubiaceae family, comprises over 90 species. These plants are typically shrubs or small trees, native to subtropical Africa and southern Asia. The seeds of certain Coffea species are used to produce coffee, and these seeds are commonly referred to as beans in the trade. Coffee beans are cultivated extensively in tropical regions, both for local consumption and export to temperate countries. Coffee is one of the world's most significant commodity crops and serves as a primary export product for several nations. The coffee plant can grow up to 5 meters (10–12 feet) in height and is resilient to severe pruning. However, it cannot thrive in areas with winter frost. Optimal growth occurs at high elevations, where the plants require substantial amounts of water and fertilizer to maximize coffee berry yields, which range from 800 to 1400 kilograms per hectare. To mitigate soil acidity, which can result from mineral runoff in mountainous areas, calcium carbonate and other lime minerals are sometimes applied. The caffeine content in coffee beans acts as a natural defense mechanism, deterring many creatures from consuming the seeds, similar to how nicotine functions in tobacco leaves. Among the various Coffea species, Coffea arabica is regarded as producing the highest quality beans. Other species, such as Coffea canephora (var. robusta), are cultivated on land unsuitable for Coffea arabica. The coffee tree produces red or purple fruits (drupes), each containing two seeds, which are the coffee beans. In approximately 5–10% of coffee cherry crops, a single seed, known as a peaberry, is found instead of the usual two. Peaberries are smaller and rounder than regular coffee beans and are sometimes claimed to have a distinct flavor profile, though this is debated. Peaberries are often separated from the main yield and sold separately or discarded. The coffee tree begins to bear fruit after 3–5 years and continues to do so for about 50–60 years, though some trees can live up to 100 years. The blossoms of the coffee tree resemble jasmine in color and fragrance, and the fruit takes approximately nine months to ripen. Globally, an estimated 15 billion coffee trees are cultivated on 100,000 square kilometers of land. Coffee also serves as a food source for the larvae of certain butterfly and moth species, such as Dalceridae, Turnip Moth, and some Endoclita species. In its natural habitat, Coffea grows under shade. However, most commercial coffee is produced on full-sun plantations, often established through deforestation. Shade-grown coffee naturally mulches its environment, has a longer lifespan than sun-grown varieties, and depletes fewer soil resources. Some believe shade-grown coffee is of higher quality, as the smaller cherries produced under shade concentrate the flavors into the seed (bean). Additionally, shade-grown coffee supports environmentally friendly ecosystems, providing habitats for a greater variety and number of migratory birds compared to sun-grown coffee farms. The term green coffee bean refers to both mature and immature coffee beans that have undergone wet or dry processing to remove the pulp and mucilage, leaving an intact wax layer on the outer surface. These beans range in color from green to brown or yellow and weigh between 300 and 330 milligrams per dried bean. Green coffee beans contain non-volatile and volatile compounds that attract insects but deter animals from consuming the fruit and seeds. These compounds also contribute to the flavor of roasted coffee beans. Among the non-volatile compounds, nitrogenous compounds, carbohydrates, and lipids play significant roles in the aroma and biological activity of roasted coffee. Caffeine, a key alkaloid, is present in both green and roasted coffee beans, with concentrations ranging from 1% to 2.5% by weight in dried green coffee. The caffeine content remains stable during bean maturation. Other alkaloids, such as theophylline, theobromine, paraxanthine, liberine, and methylliberine, are present in lower concentrations. Caffeine is odorless but has a bitter taste, which is masked by organic acids in green coffee. Trigonelline, a derivative of vitamin B6, is another nitrogenous compound found in green coffee beans, with concentrations between 0.6% and 1% by weight. During roasting, trigonelline is largely degraded into nicotinic acid (vitamin B3), leaving only small amounts of the original molecule in roasted beans. Proteins, accounting for 8–12% of the dry weight of green coffee beans, are primarily composed of 11-S storage proteins, which degrade into free amino acids during bean maturation. These amino acids contribute to the bitter taste of green coffee and are absent in roasted beans. Carbohydrates make up about 50% of the dry weight of green coffee beans, with polysaccharides such as arabinogalactan, galactomannan, and cellulose dominating the carbohydrate fraction. Arabinogalactan, which constitutes up to 17% of the dry weight, has immunomodulating properties by stimulating the body's cellular defense system. Free monosaccharides, such as glucose, fructose, and galactose, are present in mature green coffee beans. Mannitol, a powerful scavenger of hydroxyl radicals, is also found in green coffee. Lipids, which are non-polar and hydrophobic, account for 11.7–14 grams per 100 grams of dried green coffee. These lipids include linoleic acid, palmitic acid, oleic acid, stearic acid, arachidic acid, diterpenes, triglycerides, and esters. Arabica beans have a higher lipid content than robusta beans. Diterpenes, such as cafestol and kahweol, make up about 20% of the lipid fraction and are known for their protective effects on liver tissue against chemical oxidation. Chlorogenic acids, a group of polyphenols with antioxidant properties, are present in green coffee beans, with robusta beans containing 65 milligrams per gram and arabica beans containing 140 milligrams per gram. These acids are largely destroyed during roasting, leaving less than 30 milligrams per gram in roasted beans. Chlorogenic acids enhance caffeine solubility and modulate taste, contributing to the bitter and sour flavors of coffee. Volatile compounds in green coffee beans, such as short-chain fatty acids, aldehydes, and nitrogen-containing aromatic molecules, are responsible for the unpleasant odor and taste of green coffee. These compounds can cause nausea and vomiting, making green coffee unsuitable for direct consumption. Roasting neutralizes most of these unpleasant compounds and generates the characteristic aroma of coffee. However, roasting also destroys beneficial molecules like antioxidants and vitamins. Green coffee beans are a rich source of antioxidants, such as polyphenols and mannitol, which protect against chemical peroxidation. Extracts of green coffee have been shown to improve vascular reactivity in humans. However, due to the unpleasant odor of volatile compounds, green coffee is typically consumed in coated capsules rather than as a beverage.
